Election official turnover has been increasing steadily over the past 25 years, reflecting the growing complexity and demands of election administration.
The Bipartisan Policy Center released a report in 2024 showing that turnover rose from 28% in 2004 to 39% in 2022.
This updated analysis, produced in partnership with Joshua Ferrer and Daniel M.
Thompson of UCLA, extends that work through the November 2024 election, providing new insights into the challenges facing America’s election workforce.
*   Election official turnover has increased steadily since 2000 but is increasing faster since 2020.
*   Rising turnover means less time spent in a role.
Despite less time in their role, many new election officials have prior experience in election administration.
*   A long-term increase in turnover is limited to small jurisdictions, but recently, large jurisdictions have seen more pronounced rises in turnover.
*   Turnover is increasing nationwide, with state-by-state variations in turnover driven largely by the number of jurisdictions in a state.

Although election administration is resilient in the face of change and turnover does not have a significant impact on election performance, state and federal action is needed to address the chronic and emerging causes of turnover.

2024 saw the highest recorded rate of turnover in at least the past quarter century: 41% of election officials administering the presidential election were different from those who ran the presidential election four years prior.
There are a number of explanations for the recent increase in turnover, which we explore in detail in our 2024 report.

These factors include heightened hostility toward election officials, the increasing complexity of election administrators’ duties, and an aging population of election officials, many of whom are retiring.
Previously, we reported that turnover rates in 2020 were slightly higher than the gradually increasing long-term trend would predict.
We are now confident that recent increases in the departure rate of local election officials are above the trend.
In other words, election officials have been leaving at higher rates over the past two decades.
Since the 2020 presidential election, however, the rate of departures has grown significantly more quickly.

This means that high turnover rates are due to both long-term causes—which explain the gradually increasing turnover rates since 2000—and to recent causes, which explain the especially fast-rising departures over the past few years.
In 2006, 60% of chief local election officials had been in their role for six or more years, but by 2022, this percentage had fallen to 53%.
In 2024, only 47% of chief local election officials had been in their role for six or more years.

Similarly, the percentage of officials with experience administering a presidential election has decreased: 72% of chief local election officials who administered the 2004 election had previously administered at least one presidential election.
Our updated data reveal that in 2024, just 60% of election officials had previously overseen the administration of a presidential election in their jurisdiction.
Despite increasing turnover and loss of experience, the majority of chief election officials still have experience running at least one presidential election cycle.
This is important because presidential elections typically see the highest turnout and are the most visible elections administered.
The 2024 EVIC Survey of Local Election Officials found that the average official has served seven years in their current position but possesses 11 years of total service in the field.

This means that before assuming the chief position, officials have typically served in election administration roles, where they gained valuable on-the-job experience that prepared them for their new role.
Encouragingly, these averages have held stable for the past few iterations of the EVIC survey.

To further investigate the experience of new election officials, we searched for public reports on the professional backgrounds of all election officials who took over their office before the 2020 or 2022 general elections and served in offices responsible for all or nearly all election administration duties in their jurisdiction.
We found background information on 343 of the 441 officials who meet these criteria.
N early 60% of new officials have prior professional experience in elections, according to our findings We also find that nearly 80% have experience in government.
In other words, new local election officials tend to have relevant experience in elections or government that better prepares them to administer successful elections.
A more comprehensive summary of the methodological approach to this analysis can be found in Ferrer and Thompson’s 2025 paper, Does Leader Turnover Degrade Local Government Performance?
Evidence from Local Election Officials.

The overall trend of increasing turnover masks two distinct trends between small and large jurisdictions: a gradual increase in turnover in small jurisdictions, and a more sudden spike in large jurisdictions.
Ninety-three percent of jurisdictions have fewer than 100,000 voting-age residents.
The rate of turnover in these jurisdictions is similar to the overall trend and has been increasing gradually over time.
While turnover rates in these smaller jurisdictions are at record highs, the rate of increase is not significantly higher in recent years relative to the long-term trend.
Meanwhile, turnover in large jurisdictions did not increase significantly between 2004 and 2020, averaging around 35% during this period.
However, starting in 2020, turnover in populous jurisdictions has risen dramatically, resulting in turnover rates above 45% following the 2020 election cycle.
In general, turnover rates in jurisdictions with at least 100,000 voting-age residents are higher than turnover rates in less populous jurisdictions.
One encouraging sign is that 2024 was the first year since 2018 that the turnover rate of chief election officials in the country’s most populous jurisdictions did not increase.
The four-year turnover rate decreased slightly, from 46.1% in 2022 to 45.6% in 2024.
Increasing turnover is happening across the country and is not limited to one geographic region or due to a state- or region-specific cause.
Although turnover has increased steadily in small jurisdictions and only more recently in large ones, turnover has risen at relatively similar rates across regions.
This suggests we need nationwide solutions to reduce turnover rates and to increase the retention of high-quality election administrators.
Turnover has increased over the past 20 years in the Northeast, Midwest, South, and West, with each region seeing a spike since 2018.
The trends are widespread and are not limited to one or two regions.
Even this broad geographic analysis reveals idiosyncratic rises and falls over time, which are likely due to statistical noise with smaller sample sizes.

State-level turnover rates are much more variable due to the smaller number of jurisdictions in each state, making it easy to mistakenly attribute year-to-year swings in turnover to specific factors rather than statistical randomness.
For this reason, we focus on national turnover rates and trends in this report.
Turnover has increased over time across all regions of the country, across both county-administered and municipal-administered election jurisdictions, and among both elected and appointed officials.
This means that addressing increasing turnover requires national solutions rather than a state-by-state approach.

Despite increasing turnover of election officials, there are reasons for optimism about the resiliency of the U.S. election system.
Although more chief election officials are new to the job than in the past, the majority are not.
At present, 60% of chief local election officials have experience administering a presidential election, and nearly half have been in their role for at least six years.
Additionally, almost all new officials possess relevant experience, including government employment and previous professional work administering elections.
W e have also found that election performance is remarkably resilient in the face of leadership changes.
Ferrer and Thompson’s forthcoming paper in the American Journal of Political Science analyzes the effects of turnover on the quality of election administration.
They find that turnover of a chief local election official does not meaningfully affect most observable indicators of performance.
Jurisdictions under new administration have similar levels of voter turnout, residual votes, and provisional ballot rates.
Residents do not report more problems at the polls after a leadership transition, nor is there any observable decrease in voter confidence that the election was administered properly.
The one possible exception to these findings is wait times: It appears voters wait slightly longer on average to vote after turnover.
Our second takeaway is more cautionary.
It is clear that election official turnover has increased substantially over the past two decades—by roughly 13 percentage points, or 45%—and this increase has accelerated over the past few years.
This means we need new policies and strategies to support election officials and address both the long-term and the more recent increases.
We lay out policies and strategies to address turnover in our 2024 report.

The recommendations for election officials and for state and federal legislatures deal with both the election workforce’s immediate needs and ways to promote stable election official turnover in the long term.
To assess whether the trend break we observe in recent years is out of the ordinary, we conduct two analyses.

First, we use a simple linear regression to predict the turnover rate in 2022 and 2024 using data from 2004 to 2020 and ask whether observed turnover in recent years is statistically distinguishable from the turnover rate predicted by the observed trend.
We find that the observed turnover rate in 2022 and 2024 is indeed statistically distinguishable from the turnover rate predicted by the observed trend.
Second, we extend this analysis back in time, asking whether observed turnover in 2014, 2016, 2018, and 2020 is noticeably higher or lower than the trend in turnover prior to that year would predict.
Figure A.1 presents the results of this.

We find that among the last six election cycles from 2014-2024, 2022 and 2024 are the largest breaks in election official turnover at 4 percentage points higher than expected, and they are statistically distinguishable from the existing trend.
However, they are not the only recent out-of-line breaks in turnover rates.
Turnover was 2.6 percentage points higher than expected in 2016 based on existing trends, and the observed turnover in both 2014 and 2016 is statistically distinguishable from the trend.
Our methods for measuring election official turnover are identical to what was stated in BPC’s previous report, except in two respects.
First, our dataset is now larger.
In total, our data encompasses 19,679 local chief election officials across 6,290 jurisdictions.
This is by far the largest collection of data on election officials ever undertaken.
Table A.1 details which local election officials are captured in each state.
Second, we now collect snapshots of local officials for 2024 as close to the November general election as possible.
This makes our observations of turnover in 2024 comparable to previous turnover measurements.

The Election Workforce Advisory Council, co-administered by The Elections Group, is an interdisciplinary group of election officials, academics, and workforce experts focused on enhancing and innovating recruitment, retention, and training within election administration.

The Task Force on Elections, first convened by BPC in 2019, is a geographically and politically diverse group of state and local election officials devoted to creating durable, pragmatic policies that advance secure, accessible, and trustworthy elections.
